questions.stem: In Palantir's vocabulary, what differentiates a Forward Deployed Engineer from a traditional 'Dev'?

choices.text: An FDE builds many capabilities for one customer
An FDE builds one capability for many customers; a Dev builds many capabilities for one customer
An FDE works remotely; a Dev works on-site at the office
An FDE writes documentation; a Dev writes production code

questions.explanation: The Pragmatic Engineer framing is explicit: a Dev builds one capability for many customers (a product feature), while an FDE builds many capabilities for one customer, in their environment. The reversed-direction distractor (A) is the common trap if you only half-remember the contrast.

sources.title: FDE role — three definitions worth holding together

questions.stem: Which of these best characterises the FDE's primary deliverable at a client engagement?

choices.text: A recommendation slide deck the client implements
A signed Statement of Work for the next phase of consulting
Working code in the client's environment that the client runs after the FDE leaves
A reference architecture document for the client's internal team

questions.explanation: The reading contrasts FDEs explicitly with sales engineers (whose deliverable is the sale), management consultants (slide decks), and solutions architects (reference architectures). The FDE's deliverable is working code in production. A is the consultant antipattern; D is the solutions-architect one — both are tempting because they describe adjacent roles.

sources.title: FDE role — three definitions worth holding together

questions.stem: Which phase of the three-phase Karsun-FDE programme arc does the 6-week intensive sit inside?

choices.text: Phase 3 — on-the-job development
Phase 2 — the intensive itself
Phase 1 — pre-cohort foundation
Phase 0 — recruiting and screening

questions.explanation: Phase 1 is the async pre-cohort foundation (Java/Python, Git, LLM intro), Phase 2 is this 6-week intensive, Phase 3 is six months of on-the-job development with monthly coach check-ins. Phase 0 is not part of the named arc.

questions.stem: Which of the following are named in the 12 FDE situations vocabulary used across the programme? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: Tech-stack comprehension
Requirements synthesis
Pair programming style preference
6R and system mapping
Hiring loop design

questions.explanation: The 12 situations are: data comprehension, tech-stack comprehension, requirements synthesis, estimation, 6R/system mapping, NFRs, cloud thinking, DevOps thinking, database thinking, security thinking, architecture thinking, design thinking. Pair-programming style and hiring-loop design are not in the vocabulary — they may be valuable engineering concerns, but they aren't the FDE-situation framing the programme uses.

questions.stem: Claude Code's value at a federal client is that it writes more code per hour than a junior engineer.

choices.text: Yes — code-generation throughput is the explicit Day-1 metric in the reading
Yes — the reading frames Claude Code's value as a replacement for engineering effort
Yes — the FDE situations list 'code-generation speed' as situation #4
The value is faster comprehension of unfamiliar systems — replacing grep with English questions you verify against source
The value is that Claude Code blocks production deploys until tests pass
The value is that Claude Code automatically generates ADRs for every architectural decision

questions.explanation: The Claude Code reading frames the muscle being trained as ask-the-codebase-questions-and-verify, not generate-code-faster. Federal codebases are often years-old, original engineers gone, READMEs stale; the comprehension-accelerant property is the value. Code generation is incidental.

questions.stem: Which of the four Claude Code extensibility surfaces is appropriate for a workflow that 'must execute every time, regardless of model interpretation' — for example, blocking commits that contain AWS access keys?

choices.text: Custom Skill (slash-command workflow)
MCP server (external-system bridge)
Subagent (isolated context window)
Hook (PreToolUse on Bash)

questions.explanation: The morphllm 2026 guide quoted in the reading names the principle: 'Hooks guarantee execution; prompts do not.' Skills are model-routed and may be skipped under context pressure. Hooks are shell scripts that fire deterministically on every matching event — the right surface for security guardrails. MCP servers expose external tools; Subagents isolate context.

sources.title: Why this matters for federal clients

questions.stem: You walk into an unfamiliar Karsun client repo on Day 1. Which two files should you read first to understand what's wired into Claude Code?

choices.text: .mcp.json and .claude/settings.json
package.json and Dockerfile
README.md and CONTRIBUTING.md
.env and .gitignore

questions.explanation: The Best Practices section says it explicitly: '.mcp.json' lists external systems Claude can access, and '.claude/settings.json' declares active hooks. Together they reveal the system's external surface plus its guardrails. README/CONTRIBUTING are descriptive but not Claude-Code-configurative; .env is blocked from reads by default.

questions.stem: A Skill's SKILL.md has a vague description field like 'deploy stuff'. What is the most likely consequence?

choices.text: Claude will treat it as a high-priority skill and auto-invoke for every deploy-related task
Claude will refuse to load it until the description is rewritten
Claude will ignore it at routing time and the skill will only run when invoked manually
Claude will rewrite the description automatically based on the skill body

questions.explanation: The reading quotes the 2026 ofox.ai guide: 'Write skill descriptions like API tool definitions — they're the contract Claude uses for routing.' Vague descriptions get ignored at auto-routing; the skill becomes manual-only. Distractors A/B/D anthropomorphise behaviour Claude doesn't have.

questions.stem: Which of the following are appropriate use cases for a `PreToolUse` hook in Claude Code? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: Blocking reads of .env, *.pem, and *.key files
Blocking `cat .env` or `printenv` invocations in Bash
Orchestrating a multi-step PR-review workflow with stakeholder sign-off
Blocking writes that contain JWT / AWS-key / PEM-block patterns
Connecting Claude to a Jira ticketing system

questions.explanation: Hooks are appropriate when you need deterministic execution — secret-file blocks, dangerous-command blocks, write-pattern checks. Multi-step workflows belong in Skills (judgement required). External-system connectivity belongs in MCP servers. C and E are the classic surface-mismatch traps.

questions.stem: What is the canonical reason to delegate work to a Subagent instead of running it in the main Claude conversation?

choices.text: Subagents have access to tools the main conversation can't use
Heavy parallel work runs in an isolated context window
Subagents are billed at a lower rate than the main conversation
Subagents bypass all hooks and run with full privileges

questions.explanation: The reading describes subagents as 'sub-conversation with its own context window' — appropriate for batch / parallel / heavy work that would otherwise crowd out the main task. The Riot 'balance-tester subagent' example is the canonical pattern. D is dangerously wrong — subagents respect hooks.

questions.stem: Which traffic axis does an API gateway primarily handle in a microservices system?

choices.text: East-west — service-to-service communication inside the network
Database-only traffic between application tiers and the storage layer
All inter-process communication, including same-host messaging
North-south — external clients (browsers, mobile, partners) to backend services

questions.explanation: Kong's framing quoted in the reading: 'An API gateway handles north-south traffic (client-to-service), while a service mesh manages east-west traffic (service-to-service).' These two axes need different controls because they have different threat models and latency budgets.

questions.stem: Which of these are capabilities an API gateway provides at the edge of a microservices system, per the reading? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: Authentication (JWT/OAuth2, mTLS, API keys)
Per-tenant rate limiting and quota enforcement
Automatic database schema migrations
Tenant resolution (JWT claim or hostname → tenant)
Background job scheduling (cron-style)

questions.explanation: The reading's gateway-capabilities table lists auth, rate limiting, routing/versioning, tenant resolution, payload transformation, observability, and circuit-breaking. Schema migrations belong to the database/IaC layer; background-job scheduling is a worker concern. Both C and E are domain-plausible but live outside the gateway's responsibility.

sources.title: What an API gateway actually does

questions.stem: For a 4-service training system like `acquire-gov`, what does the reading say about deploying a service mesh?

choices.text: Overengineering — mesh operational cost doesn't pay off below ~15 services
A service mesh is mandatory for any system with more than one service
A service mesh replaces the API gateway in small systems
A service mesh is required for FedRAMP authorization

questions.explanation: The CloudNativeNow trend quoted in the reading: the mesh's cost (control-plane management, sidecar overhead) does not pay off until ~15+ services. For four services, gateway + direct service-to-service is sufficient. D is invented — FedRAMP makes no mesh requirement.

sources.title: What a service mesh adds beyond a gateway

questions.stem: Inside a docker-compose network, how should the `api-gateway` service reach `orders-service` running in another container on port 8081?

choices.text: http://localhost:8081 — the compose network proxies it transparently
http://host.docker.internal:8081
http://orders-service:8081 — using the container's compose-DNS name
http://127.0.0.1:8081 with the container ID as a header

questions.explanation: Inside the compose network, services resolve each other by container/service name — `orders-service:8081`. The reading is explicit: 'localhost inside a container is the container itself.' A and D both attempt to use loopback addressing which would point to the gateway container, not orders.

questions.stem: A monolith can be 6R-mapped just as flexibly as a microservices mesh.

choices.text: Yes — 6R applies uniformly to any application regardless of architecture
Yes — the 6Rs are about business outcomes, not deployment shape
Yes — monoliths can be migrated piece-by-piece using strangler-fig pattern
6R is per-service in microservices but all-or-nothing in monoliths — every 6R decision becomes a single yearlong bet
Monoliths require Retire as the only R; nothing else applies
6R is for cloud-native systems only

questions.explanation: The reading frames the modernization angle explicitly: a monolith makes 'replatform one piece' a year-long migration; microservices makes it a two-week PR. 6R applied to a service is mix-and-match; applied to a monolith it is an all-or-nothing decision. That's the structural difference. T3 is tempting because strangler-fig exists, but it's a way to *decompose* the monolith first — not a way to 6R the monolith as-is.

sources.title: Why microservices at all — the modernization angle

questions.stem: Per the reading, which four JWT claims/checks does every JWT-validating API gateway perform?

choices.text: signature, scope, role, tenant
signature, iss, aud, exp
issuer, audience, scope, nonce
signature, exp, nbf, jti

questions.explanation: Signature (anti-tampering), `iss` (correct issuer), `aud` (this API, not a sibling), `exp` (still fresh). The reading calls these the ~95% of the security story. Scope/role/tenant are application-level concerns; nbf/jti exist in RFC 7519 but aren't the gateway's four canonical checks.

sources.title: What the gateway actually checks — four claims

questions.stem: Why does checking `aud` (audience) matter — what does it specifically protect against?

choices.text: Tokens whose signature was forged by a third party
Tokens missing the `Bearer` prefix in the Authorization header
Tokens that have expired in transit between client and gateway
Tokens issued by your trusted IdP, but for a different application of yours

questions.explanation: Audience prevents cross-API token reuse: a token issued by your IdP for the reporting API should not be accepted by the orders API. Signature handles forgery; exp handles expiry; the Bearer prefix is parsing, not validation. The classic failure mode — accepting `iss` and `exp` but skipping `aud` — lets every sibling-API token in.

questions.stem: The api-gateway validates a JWT successfully and forwards the request to the orders-service. Should orders-service re-validate the JWT or trust the gateway's decision?

choices.text: Re-validate (at minimum re-check iss + aud) — defence-in-depth against gateway compromise
Trust the gateway — re-validation duplicates work and adds latency for no security gain
Trust the gateway only if mTLS is used between gateway and service
Only re-validate when the request modifies state (POST/PUT/DELETE), not on reads

questions.explanation: The reading is explicit: downstream services must not blindly trust forwarded headers. Defence-in-depth requires re-validation (or at minimum iss + aud check). The 'lazy-trust failure mode' is the most common authorisation flaw auditors flag. C is the tempting half-right — mTLS authenticates the transport but doesn't validate the *user* token.

questions.stem: What does a correlation ID enable in a distributed microservices system that's impossible without it?

choices.text: Authenticating the user without checking JWT
Encrypting log payloads at rest in CloudWatch
Stitching N service log streams back to a single inbound request
Replaying the request idempotently if the gateway crashes

questions.explanation: Microsoft's playbook (quoted in the reading): a correlation ID makes it 'easier to correlate logs across multiple components.' Without it, you have N separate log streams with no shared identifier. Encryption, auth, and idempotent replay are unrelated concerns that may co-exist but aren't what the correlation ID solves.

questions.stem: A monolith's free-text logs work fine because you can grep one stream. Why doesn't that approach scale to a 6-service microservices system?

choices.text: grep is too slow on log files larger than 100MB
Each service logs at its own cadence with no shared identifier
Microservices systems can't use grep because logs are binary-encoded
Each service uses a different logging framework and they're not interoperable

questions.explanation: The reading: 'service A logs ... then service B logs ... with no obvious connection between them in the interleaved log output.' The fix is structured (JSON) logs + correlation ID — *both* parts. A and C are technically wrong; D is overstated (frameworks differ but logs can still be aggregated).

questions.stem: Which header is the OpenTelemetry-standard carrier for distributed-trace context across service boundaries?

choices.text: X-Trace-ID
Authorization
X-Forwarded-For
traceparent (W3C)

questions.explanation: The W3C `traceparent` header is the OpenTelemetry/W3C standard for propagating trace ID + span ID across services. The reading recommends pairing it with `X-Correlation-ID` for tooling-vendor portability. `X-Trace-ID` is a vendor-specific variant that predates the W3C standard.

questions.stem: A `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` uses `aws-access-key-id: ${{ secrets.AWS_KEY }}`. What's the primary security failure mode the OIDC pattern addresses?

choices.text: Long-lived credentials leak via CI logs and outlast departed employees
The IAM key gets rotated too often and breaks deploys
GitHub Secrets has a 64KB size limit
AWS doesn't support IAM users for programmatic access anymore

questions.explanation: The reading lists the failure modes: secrets leak through CI logs, exfiltrated from developer machines, get committed by mistake; credentials remain valid until manually rotated; departed-employee access lingers because there's no expiry. OIDC replaces this with per-workflow-run short-lived tokens. C and D are invented; A is the inverse problem.

sources.title: The antipattern: long-lived cloud keys as CI secrets

questions.stem: Converting a workflow from long-lived AWS keys to OIDC requires which of the following workflow-side changes? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: Add `permissions: id-token: write` to the workflow
Replace `aws-access-key-id`/`aws-secret-access-key` with `role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::...:role/...`
Remove the `secrets.AWS_KEY`/`AWS_SECRET` references
Add a self-hosted runner — OIDC isn't supported on GitHub-hosted runners
Set `runs-on: aws-runners` instead of `ubuntu-latest`

questions.explanation: The reading's hands-on exercise answer enumerates A/B/C exactly. D is wrong — GitHub-hosted runners are the standard OIDC client; in fact most OIDC docs assume them. E is invented.

sources.title: The workflow side — three load-bearing lines

questions.stem: What is the default session-credential lifetime returned by AWS STS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` when no override is set?

choices.text: 15 minutes
12 hours
1 hour
Until the workflow completes

questions.explanation: AWS STS defaults to 3600 s (1 hour); valid range is 15 min (900 s) to 12 hr (43200 s). The reading recommends defaulting to the lowest tolerable value for the deploy — 15–60 min for most jobs.

sources.title: The workflow side — three load-bearing lines

questions.stem: An IAM role's trust policy has `StringLike: "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/my-repo:*"`. Why is this a security concern the reading flags?

choices.text: `StringLike` is deprecated; use `StringEquals` only
Any branch (including feature branches and forks) can assume the role — defeats OIDC scoping
It doesn't include the `aud` claim, so STS will reject all assumptions
It uses an `arn:aws:iam` prefix instead of the OIDC-specific prefix

questions.explanation: The freecodecamp guide quoted in the reading flags exactly this: leaving `:sub` as `repo:org/repo:*` (wildcard branch) defeats the scoping argument. Trust policies should scope to the specific branch (or branch pattern) that should be allowed to deploy. A is invented; C and D are syntactically wrong.

sources.title: The IAM trust policy — where scoping actually happens

questions.stem: Your application's IAM role grants `bedrock:InvokeModel`, but calls to Claude on Bedrock fail with a model-access error in the response body (not an IAM AccessDenied). What layer is the problem at?

choices.text: Code-level IAM — re-attach the policy
Network — the VPC doesn't have a Bedrock endpoint
Region — Claude isn't available in any AWS region
Account-level model entitlement

questions.explanation: Two layers: IAM-level permission and account-level entitlement. IAM failures return AccessDeniedException; entitlement failures return a model-access message. The smoke test is `aws bedrock list-foundation-models` — if Anthropic models don't appear, it's an entitlement ticket. C is wrong (Claude is available in us-east-1 and others); D is a real concern but not what the response-body error indicates.

sources.title: Cloud-LLM model access — a separate concern

questions.stem: Granting `bedrock:InvokeModel` to your application's IAM role is sufficient to start calling Claude models on Bedrock.

choices.text: Yes — `bedrock:InvokeModel` is the only IAM action required for end-to-end Bedrock access
Yes — Anthropic models are enabled by default in all AWS accounts since 2024
Yes — once IAM grants the action, the AWS provider handles model availability transparently
Account-level model entitlement (Bedrock console 'Model access' page) must also be granted — IAM permission alone returns model-access errors
You also need a Bedrock VPC endpoint, regardless of model entitlement
Bedrock requires a long-lived API key in addition to IAM

questions.explanation: Two layers, both must hold: account-level entitlement (Bedrock console approves Anthropic-model access) + code-level IAM (the application's role can call bedrock:InvokeModel). One without the other produces the canonical Day-1 mystery — 'permissions look right but calls fail.'

sources.title: Cloud-LLM model access — a separate concern

questions.stem: Per the reading, why is brownfield engineering the default mode of work at a federal-systems integrator?

choices.text: Federal clients carry inherited stacks, live SLAs, and legacy data — greenfield is exceptional
Federal contracts forbid greenfield builds by statute
Federal agencies pay more for brownfield work than greenfield work
Greenfield projects require FedRAMP authorisation; brownfield doesn't

questions.explanation: The IBM Think framing: brownfield projects build on existing systems 'without starting from zero.' At federal clients, the constraints — live users, SLAs, legacy data, inherited stack — make greenfield exceptional. The engineering muscles for brownfield (comprehension, risk modelling, incremental change) are what the programme trains.

questions.stem: Which of these are among the five canonical debt categories the reading identifies in any brownfield system? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: Code-level (anti-patterns, dead code, duplicated logic)
Architecture-level (wrong service boundaries, gateway-bypass paths)
Branding-level (outdated marketing materials)
Dependency / supply-chain (outdated library versions, EOL frameworks)
Pricing-tier (incorrect SaaS pricing rules)

questions.explanation: The five canonical: code-level, architecture-level, infrastructure/deployment, dependency/supply-chain, security/compliance. McKinsey adds a sixth — knowledge debt (senior engineers carrying systems in their heads). Branding and pricing are business concerns, not technical-debt categories.

sources.title: The five debt categories every brownfield system has

questions.stem: What does the reading call the dominant antipattern in modernization conversations?

choices.text: Investing in too many junior engineers instead of senior ones
Over-investing in greenfield rewrites instead of incremental improvement
Jumping to fix visible debt without first inventorying the landscape — produces whack-a-mole
Mandating Agile methodology when Waterfall would fit better

questions.explanation: McKinsey calls it the 'vicious cycle': every fix produces two new urgencies because changes ripple through unmapped dependencies. The arXiv survey: teams jump to *visible* debt without holding the rest of the landscape in view. Inventory precedes prioritisation, which precedes fixing.

questions.stem: The six standard inventory dimensions in the reading are: artefact, location, category, severity, effort, and ___?

choices.text: Assigned engineer
Suggested R (mapping to 6R/7R)
Estimated cost in dollars
Detected date (when first found)

questions.explanation: The six are: artefact, location, category, severity, effort, suggested-R. Suggested-R explicitly maps each debt item to one of Retain/Rehost/Replatform/Refactor/Repurchase/Retire so prioritisation can happen later. A/C/D are reasonable extra dimensions but aren't the canonical six.

questions.stem: Which of these is a properly-formed inventory item per the reading's bar?

choices.text: 'Improve security'
'Modernize the backend'
'Add more test coverage'
'JWT signature validation skipped if header malformed in api-gateway/SecurityConfig.java:41'

questions.explanation: The reading's Best Practices: 'Inventory items are short and specific. "Improve security" is not an inventory item; "JWT signature validation skipped if header malformed in `api-gateway/SecurityConfig.java:41`" is.' The others are aspirational goals, not actionable items with location.

questions.stem: In a four-service brownfield system, the same modernization initiative can produce different 6R verdicts per service (e.g., Retain the gateway, Replatform the evaluation-service, Retire the legacy reporting-service). Why does the reading emphasise this?

choices.text: Because per-service decomposition enables per-service 6R
Because the 6R framework requires at least three different Rs per project
Because federal procurement statutes require multiple R verdicts in every contract
Because mixing Rs reduces the project's overall risk score on the audit

questions.explanation: The reading: '6R is per-service, not per-application.' A microservices mesh lets you Retain one service, Refactor another, Retire a third — each decision is bounded. A monolith collapses to a single all-or-nothing 6R bet. A and C are invented constraints; D mis-frames audit scoring.

questions.stem: Static analysis tools alone are sufficient to discover all categories of technical debt in a brownfield system.

choices.text: Yes — modern SAST tools cover all five debt categories with high accuracy
Yes — if you also pair static analysis with dependency-scanners like Dependabot
Yes — most architecture-level debt eventually shows up as code smells static analysis can catch
Static analysis can't see architecture-level debt (wrong service boundaries, missing layers) or knowledge debt — these only surface through inventory, interviews, and reading the system end-to-end
Static analysis tools are deprecated as of 2025 and shouldn't be relied on
Static analysis only works on Java, not Python or JavaScript

questions.explanation: The arXiv survey quoted in the reading: 'A large portion of technical debt … cannot be mined by analysing source code.' Static analysis covers code-style and dependency-version debt; it does not surface architectural mistakes, *missing* artefacts (documentation that should exist), or knowledge debt. Those require inventory + interviews.

questions.stem: What does the reading identify as the *structural* reason vendor-supplied comparative materials are biased — independent of vendor intent?

choices.text: Vendors hire marketing agencies who use deceptive design patterns
Vendors don't have engineers good enough to produce honest comparatives
The aggregate of self-promotion materials is selected for the vendor's interests
Federal procurement law prohibits vendors from comparing themselves to competitors

questions.explanation: Thomson Reuters quote in the reading: 'even when a vendor is honest, the aggregate of their marketing materials produces a skewed picture because every individual artefact is selected for the vendor's interests.' The three named biases — selection (only wins published), framing (vendor names favourable axes), confounding (stats without apples-to-apples baselines) — compound structurally.

sources.title: Why vendor-supplied materials are structurally biased

questions.stem: Per the reading, which of these are 'standard public-source channels' for vendor due diligence the FDE should use? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q) for public companies
G2 / TrustRadius / Gartner Peer Insights customer reviews
The vendor's sales-engineer's LinkedIn DMs
Government contract awards (USAspending.gov, FPDS)
Engineering blogs (vendor + customer)

questions.explanation: The reading lists nine standard channels: SEC filings, acquisition/fundraising announcements, government-contract data, marketplace listings, customer reviews, engineering blogs, conference talks, archived web, open positions. Backchannel DMs aren't public-source and aren't a defensible due-diligence input.

questions.stem: What does the reading mean by 'triangulate every load-bearing claim across three independent channels'?

choices.text: Cross-check the claim against the vendor's own marketing, their sales team, and their solutions architects — three internal voices
Find the claim in at least three sources that don't depend on each other (e.g., a customer engineering blog + a G2 review + a government-contract award)
Re-read the vendor's website three times to confirm the wording is consistent
Run the vendor's product through three different test environments before drawing conclusions

questions.explanation: IBCA's M&A discipline quoted in the reading: 'triangulate across at least three independent channels for any claim.' The key word is *independent* — a vendor's own claim + their conference talk are not independent. Customer voices + government data + third-party reviews are. A confuses 'three sources' with 'three independent sources' — the typical trap.

questions.stem: A vendor-comparison matrix has all six dimensions populated, but several cells say 'Better' or 'Unknown' without source citations. What does the reading call this artefact?

choices.text: An FDE-grade artefact ready to send to the client
A complete deliverable provided dimension weighting is also added
An acceptable first draft to iterate on with the vendor's salesperson
Slides, not evidence — defensible matrices source every cell and name gaps explicitly

questions.explanation: The reading: 'Comparative matrices without sources are slides; comparative matrices with sources are evidence.' And 'Gaps are named, not hidden' — explicit 'Not publicly disclosed' invites the client conversation about how to fill them. Unsourced 'Better/Worse/Unknown' is the slide-deck antipattern.

sources.title: What 'good' looks like as a deliverable

questions.stem: An FDE writes 'I am doing tech-stack comprehension on the api-gateway right now' at the top of a work block. What discipline does the reading say this expresses?

choices.text: Naming the FDE situation explicitly
Time-tracking for billable hours
Standup-status reporting for the daily 09:00 meeting
Compliance with FedRAMP audit-trail requirements

questions.explanation: Best Practices section: 'Always name the FDE situation you're in at the top of every work block.' Naming forces clarity on what kind of work you're doing — comprehension vs build vs communication. The other options are tangential concerns that don't capture the reading's framing.

questions.stem: Per the Pragmatic Engineer 2024 framing, why did the FDE role explode in demand around 2024-2025?

choices.text: Universities started producing FDE-named computer-science degree tracks
AWS released a FedRAMP-High Bedrock offering that needed embedded integration support
Enterprises bought LLM products faster than internal teams could integrate them
Remote-work norms made it cheaper to embed engineers at client sites

questions.explanation: The 2024-2025 LLM enterprise-buying wave outpaced internal integration capacity. The same pattern that drove Palantir's FDE practice in the 2010s (complex-platform integration needs embedded engineers) drove OpenAI's / Anthropic's / Ramp's hiring waves in 2024-25. The Everest Group analysis frames this as a structural shift — vendors of 'platform' software *must* run an FDE practice to scale bookings.

questions.stem: MCP servers and custom Skills serve interchangeable purposes — you can swap one for the other based on engineering preference.

choices.text: Yes — both extend Claude Code and the choice is mostly cosmetic
Yes — Skills can do everything MCP servers do, just with more configuration
Yes — MCP servers are deprecated in favour of Skills as of 2026
MCP servers expose external-system tools; Skills are multi-step workflows operating on those tools — different layers, complementary, not interchangeable
MCP servers run in the cloud; Skills run locally — they can't talk to each other
Skills require a paid Claude Code subscription; MCP servers are free

questions.explanation: The reading's Best Practices spell it out: MCP for tool-level access to external systems; Skill for multi-step workflows. The Shopify migration example is canonical — MCP server connects to Shopify Admin API (the *what's reachable*), Skill orchestrates the theme-conversion workflow (the *what to do*). Different layers; both usually needed.

questions.stem: In the request-flow story, who is responsible for minting the correlation ID — and when?

choices.text: The downstream service mints it when receiving the first request
The API gateway mints it (or accepts a strict-format upstream value) before forwarding
The SPA mints it on the client side before sending the request
The identity provider mints it when issuing the JWT

questions.explanation: Best Practices: 'Mint a correlation ID at the gateway if the request didn't come with one. Accept an upstream-supplied ID only if it matches a strict format (UUID v4).' The gateway is the right place — it's the single ingress where every request passes through. Letting downstream services mint independently produces split-history; client-side IDs are untrusted; IdPs aren't on the request path.

questions.stem: You're reading a `docker-compose.yml` and notice the `orders-service` uses `ports: ["8081:8081"]` rather than `expose: ["8081"]`. What does the reading suggest this is a red flag for?

choices.text: The service will fail its healthcheck because ports must always be internal
The service can't be reached from inside the compose network
The service is using a deprecated docker-compose v2 syntax
The service is exposed to the docker host directly, enabling gateway-bypass

questions.explanation: Best Practices: 'Expose services to the docker network with expose (internal-only) instead of ports (host-mapped) unless you need direct access.' A host-mapped port on a backend service is a gateway-bypass route — that pattern is flagged as Brownfield Debt item #5 in the example inventory. B/C/D mis-characterise the compose syntax.
